messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: checking values
parts:
Is it really necessary to check both that something is non NaN and that it is finite? Such as in normal.hpp (and many other places)

      if (!check_not_nan(function, y, "Random variable", &logp, Policy()))
        return logp;
      if (!check_finite(function, mu, "Location parameter",
                        &logp, Policy()))
        return logp;

The Boost documentation (like R)

http://www.boost.org/doc/libs/1_51_0/libs/math/doc/sf_and_dist/html/math_toolkit/utils/fpclass.html

says that

template <class T>
bool isfinite(T z); // Neither infinity nor NaN.

so it seems to me that we can avoid calling check_not_nan(). I guess the exception message will be slightly less clear

" is %1%, but must be finite!"

when %1% evaluates to nan but  that is a small price to pay to avoid an extra sweep over the values every time the function is called.

Ben

> +/- infinity.

Either the variate or parameters going to infinity will
result in -infinity log probabilities, right? Those
will cause samples to be rejected. Throwing an exception
just causes this to happen earlier rather than later.

We were also talking about CDFs. On the linear scale,
those go to 0 or 1 outside the support of the PDF.

Mathematically, you can treat a PDF as a partial function
defined on its support that is non-zero everywhere it
is defined, or you can treat it as a total function that
has zero values. Same for CDFs.

I personally have been advocating treating them as
partial functions, but everyone else seems to like
extending them.

> But if you happen to get such a value in Stan, it is going to overflow whatever is a function of it. And I
> thought overflow already caused a non-fatal exception. Maybe it depends on the policy or something?

It's not so much the exception being fatal or
non-fatal as the fact that our samplers catch
exceptison thrown by the model probability functions.

It will depend on policy, but that's not easily
configurable in RStan or Stan command line. The
settings used there throw exceptions.

In C++, you can configure the static policy to instead
return -infinity (though I believe Daniel has them
all set to return NaN -- I think we'll fix that).

- Bob

It's going to return a -infinity value.  The alternative

There seem to be lots of opinions on this.

I think Boost raises domain errors for parameters out of
domain and returns 0 for infinite variates.

To add another complication, there are some distributions (although I think none that are currently in Stan) where the range of admissible values of the random variable depends on the parameters. So, for some proposals for the parameters, some of the observed data may fall in a region where there is no mass. And we definitely need to be able to reject those proposed parameters, but otherwise it is not really a problem that should prevent the sampler from continuing.

Ben

The uniform and Pareto both have this property.
As well as anything truncated.

For instance,

only admits y between L and H. So we have to
be careful to make sure L < min(y) and

inefficient or in some cases downright intractable for
HMC/NUTS.

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] checking values

As I see it, there are two ways we can find ourselves considering a
state with log-probability of -inf:
1. Some (unconstrained) parameter is ±inf, in which case something
blew up in the simulation and we should probably consider a smaller
step size.
2. There are "holes" in the posterior that have 0 mass, in which case
decreasing the step size may help a little bit but not much (you've
got a very, very light tail) or might not help at all (you've got a
discontinuity).

(1) can happen quite naturally during adaptation. (2) suggests that
your model is making things more difficult than they need to be. I
believe we're already printing a "your posterior isn't continuous"
error during the initial step size adaptation (which tests whether
you're on the edge of a discontinuity), but maybe we should also be
printing a "your posterior has a hole in it" (or maybe something more
delicately worded) warning when we get -infs with finite parameters.

Matt

What'll they think of next?

Well, "they" have already thought of plenty of things that are, to varying degrees, challenging to implement in Stan. Conversely, I would generally say that the harder it is to make something work in Stan, the even harder it is to do MLE, or Gibbs sampling, or whatever in that situation, so Stan can provide a lot of value added in these cases.

With (x,mu,xi,sigma), the constraints are

1.  mu <= x, and

2.  if (xi < 0), then x <= mu - sigma / xi

Hypothetically, if one were going to implement this generalized Pareto distribution in Stan, would you want to call it generalized_pareto or just pareto overloaded with an extra parameter? There are lots of "generalized" distributions that add parameters to the more commonly used distributions, so we probably need to decide a policy.

The Stan code's a bit clunky:

   real<lower = mu,
        upper = if_else(xi < 0, mu - sigma / xi, positive_infinity())>  x;

I'm going to fix the behavior of upper and lower
so that we can use +infinity and -infinity as "no-op"
upper and lower bounds.

I shudder to think about the geometric consequences with
shape xi --> 0, because of the non-differentiability and the
occurence of xi in the denominator of the upper bound fraction.

In general, Stan is probably subject to numerical difficulties when a parameter appears as an exponent, denominator, or both. That is one reason I mentioned awhile back that it might be nice to have an option to increase the precision, at least for parameters. Eigen supports (albeit in unsupported) arbitrary precision via software and long doubles via hardware if the hardware / compiler supports it. But I guess at the moment, we are a bit hard-coded into doubles.

The same issue comes up if we want to support

-- unit normal (y)

-- normal precision (y|mu,tau)

Without named arguments, I'd go for verbose names.
It's easier to read code that way, but harder to

I have been working on (not pushed yet) implementing the stable distribution, which ironically can be numerically unstable.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stable_distribution

The density function cannot, in general, be written in closed form. However, Buckle

http://scholar.google.com/scholar?cluster=16815367252388880789&hl=en&as_sdt=0,33

showed that there exists a closed-form bivariate density with the same parameters, plus an auxiliary parameter vector of length N to form the second variate, such that its first marginal is a stable distribution. Buckle goes on to describe a MH / Gibbs algorithm that sounds like it would be much better and easier with HMC.

The tail fatness parameter, alpha, for a stable distribution is restricted to (0,2] except that it cannot be 1.0. For alpha values very near 1.0, numeric instability is to be expected.

I think there are two cases to be concerned about. One is that alpha in the population really is close to 1.0, in which case the stable distribution simplifies to a Cauchy (but the bivariate density seems not to simplify to anything). In that case, as long as the posterior mean is kind of close to 1.0, the user could probably just estimate a Cauchy model afterward. But the other case is that the alpha in the population is not really close to 1.0, but an alpha value very near 1.0 is accepted. In that case, we need to evaluate the log-posterior and gradient accurately enough to be able to get away from that point without having things blow up.

I can certainly push it without being able to using more than double precision. I am just saying it would hypothetically be nice to have.

Ben
